message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads and have distinct architectures.

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles a wide variety of tasks (OS, applications, networking, etc.) | Specialized for highly parallel, data‑intensive tasks – originally for rendering graphics, now also for scientific computing, machine learning, etc. |
| **Core count** | Few (typically 2–32 cores in consumer CPUs, up to hundreds in server CPUs) | Hundreds to thousands of smaller cores (e.g., 2,500+ CUDA cores in an NVIDIA RTX 3090). |
| **Core design** | Complex, high‑performance cores with deep pipelines, large caches, branch prediction, and sophisticated control logic. | Simple, lightweight cores optimized for throughput; each core does less work but many can run simultaneously. |
| **Clock speed** | Higher clock speeds (3–5 GHz) because each core does more work per cycle. | Lower clock speeds (1–1.5 GHz) because the workload is split across many cores. |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, fast access to main memory. | Smaller per‑core caches; relies on high‑bandwidth memory (HBM, GDDR6) and shared memory pools. |
| **Instruction set** | Complex instruction set (CISC) or reduced instruction set (RISC) with many features (branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution). | SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) – same instruction executed on many data elements in lockstep. |
| **Typical workloads** | Sequential tasks, branching logic, I/O, OS kernel, database queries, web servers. | Parallel tasks: rendering pixels, matrix multiplications, neural network inference/training, scientific simulations. |
| **Programming model** | Traditional CPU programming (C/C++, Java, etc.) with single‑threaded or multi‑threaded code. | GPU programming requires parallel paradigms (CUDA, OpenCL, Vulkan compute, DirectX 12 compute). |
| **Energy efficiency** | Optimized for performance per watt for general tasks. | Optimized for throughput per watt for parallel workloads. |
| **Cost & form factor** | Typically cheaper per core, integrated into motherboards or SoCs. | More expensive per core, often separate cards or integrated into SoCs for mobile devices. |

### Why the difference matters

- **Parallelism**: GPUs excel when you can break a problem into many independent, identical operations (e.g., multiplying each element of a large matrix). CPUs are better when tasks require complex decision making or have irregular memory access patterns.
- **Latency vs. throughput**: CPUs minimize latency for individual operations; GPUs maximize throughput for many operations at once.
- **Programming complexity**: Writing efficient GPU code requires understanding of memory hierarchies, thread blocks, and synchronization, whereas CPU code can often be written in a straightforward, sequential style.

In practice, modern systems often use both: the CPU handles the “control” side (managing the system, running the OS, handling user input), while the GPU handles the “data‑parallel” side (graphics rendering, AI inference, large‑scale simulations). This complementary relationship allows each processor to play to its strengths.
